A. FOUNDATIONS: AGENCY REASONING 
AND POLICYMAKING FORM
This section introduces some foundational concepts through the two 
instances when SEC v. Chenery went to the Supreme Court—the Chenery 
I case in 1943 and the Chenery II case in 1947. The first case estabhshed 
the principle that a reviewing court can uphold agency action only on the 
reasoning that the agency itself used when taking the action. This point 
apphes to judicial review of all agency action, not just rulemaking, but we 
introduce it here in Chapter 5 because the judiciary’s expectations about 
agency reasoning have shaped the rulemaking process in especially 
profound ways. The second case estabhshed the principle that every agency 
has a choice between rulemaking and case-by-case adjudication as 
alternative means for articulating general legal interpretations and 
developing general pohcies (unless the substantive statute says otherwise). 
The generality of what the agency is doing does not require it to proceed by 
rulemaking (although proceeding by adjudication does require the agency 
to consider and answer new arguments in each new adjudication, in a way 
that rulemaking could foreclose). Neither of the Chenery cases was decided 
under the Administrative Procedure Act, but the APA is generally 
understood as consistent with both of them.

Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 (PUHCA) empowered the Securities
and Exchange Commission to force changes in each company’s corporate 
structure and the redistribution of ownership rights among its investors.

The mechanism to force these changes was a “reorganization plan” that the
, 
Commission would approve by adjudicatory order. Those who controlled a
holding company could propose one or more reorganization plans to the 
Commission and negotiate with the Commission over the plan’s terms, but 
the Commission had power to make changes to the plan and the ultimate 
power to decide whether to approve it and in what form. PUHCA Sections 
7 and 11 told the Commission to approve only if the plan was not 
“detrimental to the pubfic interest or the interest of investors or 
consumers” and was “fair and equitable.”]
